clue.text: Film, hi-tech, BT released

indicators.note: letters that are released are set free from their fixed order and can be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A news item about BT launching a high-tech film.
explanation.walkthrough: THE BITCH is a 1979 British film starring Joan Collins.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the title of a movie, so the clue's opening word names its category.

clue.text: Swimming coach in river finds item of clothing

indicators.note: in tells us these letters sit inside the other word

parts.note: the Trent is a major river in the English Midlands

indicators.note: swimming suggests moving about freely, so the letters swirl into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A swimming coach in a river turns up a lost piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent is a major river in the English Midlands; 'swimming' fits the river picture but tells you to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A trench coat is a belted, double-breasted raincoat, originally worn by officers in the First World War trenches.

clue.text: Caught in the Ivel, very young eel

indicators.note: caught in means trapped inside, so the letters sit within the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A very young eel is netted in the River Ivel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ivel is a small river in Bedfordshire, England, which suits the eel picture neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: An elver is a young eel, especially one migrating upriver from the sea.

clue.text: I criticise a bum in capital city

parts.note: taken as written
to slam is to criticise harshly
taken as written
bum is informal for bad or poor, as in a bum deal

explanation.surface: A traveller complains about a layabout they met in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a noun, a vagrant or a backside, but here it is the adjective meaning poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Islamabad is the capital city of Pakistan.

clue.text: Political organisation adopting hard line with the US Congress

indicators.note: organisation means arranging things into a fresh order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A political party takes a hard line in dealing with the American Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Political organisation' reads as one phrase meaning a party; split, the first word is fodder and the second the anagram signal, taking in H and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Capitol Hill, where the Capitol building stands in Washington, is used as shorthand for the US legislature.

clue.text: Wine in tavern, endless wine

indicators.note: something endless has lost its final part, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a bar is a pub or tavern
sack is an old name for a dry white wine such as sherry

explanation.surface: Someone drinks one wine in a pub and keeps topping it up without end.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is the old wine Falstaff loves; dropping its last letter leaves SAC, giving BARSAC.
explanation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white dessert wine from a commune in the Bordeaux region of France.

clue.text: Sailor holding crowd up, producing weapon

indicators.note: holding means gripping something within, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: a mob is a crowd

explanation.surface: A sailor holds back a crowd and pulls out a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: An A-bomb is an atomic bomb, a nuclear weapon.

clue.text: Hooter goes at end of marvellous championship game

parts.note: superb means marvellous
an owl hoots, so it is a hooter

explanation.surface: A horn sounds at the end of a marvellous championship match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' suggests a horn or siren at full time, but it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The Super Bowl is the annual championship game of American football's NFL.

clue.text: Happen to score, to make the grade

parts.note: a two-word phrasal verb meaning to arise or occur
taken as written
to score a surface is to scratch it

explanation.surface: Someone hopes to happen upon a good score, to meet the required standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Both idioms mean reaching an acceptable standard; the scratch was the starting line boxers had to reach.

clue.text: Holder's jacket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a paper sleeve that holds a letter
second meaning: an outer covering or casing around something

explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive, about a holder's coat, but it stands for 'is', joining two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter's paper cover holds its contents, and any enclosing outer layer or wrapper can be called by the same word.

clue.text: Cannon and Ball?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a quick-firing automatic anti-aircraft gun
second meaning: a fluffy woollen ball worn on a hat

explanation.walkthrough: Cannon and Ball were a popular British comedy double act, so the clue reads as their names; split apart, each word is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The name was given to a rapid-firing naval gun from its sound, and also means a decorative tuft or ball of wool.

clue.text: Cannon in capital — one fired by me, originally

indicators.note: someone fired is dismissed from their post, so this letter is thrown out of the word

parts.note: Cairo is the capital of Egypt
the Roman numeral for one, which is removed

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of me

explanation.surface: A cannon in a capital city, which someone claims to have fired themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: Cairo loses its I to become CARO, then M is placed beside it to give CAROM.
explanation.definitionFit: In billiards a cannon is a shot where the cue ball strikes two balls in turn; Americans call that shot a carom.

clue.text: Legitimate, our Brent activity

indicators.note: activity suggests busy movement, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone vouches that what goes on at Brent, in London, is all above board.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone true-born is genuinely born to a status, the rightful heir, just as a legitimate child is born within marriage.

clue.text: See 8
Splitting your sides? Hospital may have to put you -- -------!

definitions.text: Hospital may have to put you
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a split side literally needs sutures, so the blank is filled by the phrase

explanation.walkthrough: The joke turns the idiom literal: sides that really split would need sewing up in hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Being helpless with laughter is described with this idiom, and a wound closed by sutures is literally in them.

clue.text: Better skill shown by PM's gardener

parts.note: greater ability or competence
Gordon Brown was the British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister's gardener shows superior skill with the shrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: PM stands for Prime Minister; Gordon Brown held the post from 2007 to 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown was the famous eighteenth-century English landscape designer of country-house parks.

clue.text: Finished up at top, surprisingly, around one, accompanied by daughter

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the rearranged letters wrap the following pieces
surprisingly hints at an unexpected outcome, so the letters land in an unexpected order

parts.note: the letters of these three words
the Roman numeral for one
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone surprisingly ended up on top, with their daughter alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters wrap around I followed by D.
explanation.definitionFit: To put paid to something is to finish it off or end it, so the past tense matches finished.

clue.text: Where accidents often occur — parking lots back abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean widely scattered, so these letters are spread out and reassembled

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Accidents keep happening near the car parks at the back of a foreign resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a reversal signal, but it is fodder; 'abroad' does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a stretch of road with a high accident rate is labelled a black spot by road-safety authorities.

clue.text: Satanist crudely drawn in book

indicators.note: something drawn out of shape has been pulled about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A rough sketch of a devil-worshipper appears as an illustration in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crudely' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'drawn' does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the 1887 novel by Arthur Conan Doyle that introduced Sherlock Holmes, so it is a book title.

clue.text: Unmarried man, composer, rejected part

parts.note: Johann Sebastian Bach, the German composer

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so this word is read from end to start

parts.note: a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: A single man, a composer, was turned down for a part.
explanation.definitionFit: A bachelor is a man who has never married, the standard sense of the word.

clue.text: Heroin planted on relative in resort

parts.note: H is slang for heroin
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Drugs were planted on a family member staying at a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'planted on' puts H above AUNT. 'Resort' suggests a holiday town but is a place one frequents.
explanation.definitionFit: A haunt is a place someone visits habitually, an old sense of resort as a frequented spot.

clue.text: King, a set behind, is broken

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written
to set something down is to put it there

explanation.surface: A king who is a set down in a tennis match is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A set behind' sounds like tennis scoring, but 'set' is just a verb meaning put, placed after K and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaput is informal, from German, for something wrecked or no longer working.

clue.text: Punter initially taking a lively interest in a horse

indicators.note: initially points at how a word starts, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of Punter
being into something means being keen on it

explanation.surface: A gambler starts taking a keen interest in a particular racehorse.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinto is a horse with patchy markings of white and another colour, a piebald or skewbald.

clue.text: Food — good spread

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to spread an ointment is to rub it on

explanation.surface: Food makes a good spread, a lavish meal laid out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' looks like a noun for a feast, but it is the verb rub.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is informal slang for food.

clue.text: Notice one present in strange metallic element

indicators.note: being present in something means sitting inside it, so these letters go within another word

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
an ad is an advertisement or public notice
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A notice reports one present in a strange metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an anagram signal, but here it is a synonym in old British slang, and it is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Radium is a radioactive metallic chemical element discovered by the Curies.

clue.text: Adult to draw off small measure if need be

parts.note: A is the film classification for adult
to tap a barrel is to draw liquid off from it
an inch is a small unit of length

explanation.surface: A grown-up drains off just a little measure when needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in an emergency or if necessary, which is what if need be also expresses.

clue.text: Bombed British house

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
house, or housey-housey, is an old British name for bingo, also called lotto

explanation.surface: A British house was destroyed by bombs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombed' looks like the Blitz, but it is slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are slang for being extremely drunk, intoxicated to the point of incapacity.

clue.text: Nondescript articles that snow damaged

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Assorted bits and pieces were ruined by the snowfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatnots are miscellaneous unnamed items or trivia, things too ordinary to be given a proper name.
